title: Glossary

terms.definition: The information and decisions the effect must support, including identity, action and consequence.
The silhouette and arrangement of masses that make an effect recognizable.
The light-to-dark structure, independent of hue.
Hue, saturation and their relationships within the effect and scene.
How visual change is distributed through the effect’s life and aligned to events.
Arrangement and hierarchy that directs attention within an effect and across the scene.
The preparatory phase before the main action; often anticipation.
Preparation that makes the following action expected and legible.
The concentrated high-intensity accent of the action or contact.
A build in intensity toward a peak; it need not appear in every effect.
Motion that continues after the principal action as energy transfers and resolves.
The designed ending in which the effect disperses or loses prominence.
Acceleration and deceleration that make timing nonuniform.
Changing proportion to communicate deformation, motion or force while preserving intended volume impression.
A curved motion path used to organize gesture or flow.
Related components move or settle at different times rather than as one rigid unit.
The recognizable outer shape, assessable without texture detail.
The dominant directional gesture of an effect or movement.
The dominant mass or gesture carrying the effect’s essential meaning.
A supporting component that strengthens the primary action without displacing it.
Fine supporting ornament; usually a candidate for reduction before primary information.
Fragmenting a solid shape or texture into irregular pieces.
Progressive removal of a shape, often through a mask, rather than uniform transparency.
A spatially varying disappearance driven by a pattern or threshold.
A post effect that spreads bright areas into surrounding pixels; it is not geometry or a damage boundary.
An appearance of self-illumination; in Roblox light emission alone does not mean light cast onto the scene.
Combining light contributions by addition, tending to brighten overlapping regions.
Combining foreground and background using transparency; ordering and overlap matter.
A sequence of images stored in a sheet or atlas and played as animation.
An image atlas containing individual frames or sprites.
An animation intended to play through once per event.
Animation that repeats; its end-to-start transition needs design.
A new drawing or pose on each frame of the stated base timebase.
A drawing or pose held for two frames of the stated base timebase; not inherently 2 fps.
Changing the number of held base frames between image updates.
A brief graphic accent at impact, which may change silhouette, colour or contrast.
A brief pause or hold associated with contact; clarify whether simulation, animation or only presentation stops.
A held image or pose; it may be cinematic rather than a gameplay-wide pause.
A directional camera displacement or rotation linked to an event.
Time-varying camera or screen movement used to reinforce an event.
In Eiserloh’s camera model, a state variable accumulated by events and decayed over time to drive shake nonlinearly.
A cue announcing an action or hazard before activation.
The gameplay geometry used to determine contact or damage; its visual indicator must represent it truthfully.
How strongly an item attracts attention relative to its context.
Impaired identification of a target because nearby visual elements interfere, especially in peripheral vision.
Visual competition that makes relevant information harder to locate or identify.
Repeated shading of overlapping pixels; broad transparent layers can make cost high.
Level of detail; a project’s method for reducing presentation cost while preserving essential information.
Avoiding rendering or updating content that is not needed under defined visibility or relevance conditions.
Reusing instances rather than repeatedly creating and destroying them; requires reliable reset and cleanup.
A flat element oriented toward the camera or another defined direction.
Information that helps communicate distance, layering or spatial relationships.
A Roblox local reference frame used to place or connect components.
A Roblox connection rendered between attachments, useful for continuous paths and arcs.
A Roblox strip generated from attachment movement over time.
A ParticleEmitter rendering-depth offset; it does not move gameplay geometry.
A ParticleEmitter control affecting particle simulation speed, separate from global gameplay time.
Common shorthand for automated photosensitive-epilepsy flash/pattern analysis; tool, version and recorded sequence must be specified.
Combining and adapting existing parts into a new effect rather than authoring every component from scratch.
Testing the main shapes, motion and timing before texture/detail polish.
Capacity to process screen pixels; a few large sprites can cost more than many tiny ones.
Compositing that preserves occluding color according to opacity.
A lower-resolution texture representation used at smaller projected sizes or under resource constraints.
Roblox flipbook mode that fits a complete cell sequence across the particle lifetime.
A drawing held for two frames of a stated presentation frame rate; not a universal update frequency.

intro: Definitions use established field terms. Cadence requires an explicit base frame rate; a frame count alone is not a duration. Engine property names remain distinct from perceptual quantities.
